---
title: "The Table contract"
---

`Phibble\Contracts\Table` is the interface that every table backend
implements. phplyr's verbs call its methods, so a pipeline runs unchanged on
any backend. phibble ships two implementations: `Frame`, which holds data in
PHP arrays, and `SqlTable`, which compiles verbs to SQL. phpolars implements it
over Polars.

This page is for authors of backends. It lists the rules that every
implementation follows and the semantics of each method.

## Rules

- **Immutability.** Every method returns a new table and leaves the original
  unchanged.
- **Return types.** Verbs are declared to return `Table`. A backend may return
  a different implementation. `SqlTable` returns a `Frame` when it falls back to
  memory for a closure. `Frame` declares `static`.
- **NA.** PHP `null` is NA in every column type.
- **Grouping.** `groupBy()` records grouping columns as metadata. `filter()`,
  `mutate()`, `mutateGroups()`, `filterGroups()`, `summarise()`, and
  `eachGroup()` work per group. The other verbs keep the grouping.
- **Group order.** Groups are visited in sorted key order, as in dplyr:
  ascending, factors by level order, NA last, and strings in byte order.
  `filter()`, `mutate()`, and `arrange()` keep the input row order.
- **Rowwise tables.** `rowwise()` makes every row its own group, in row order.
  `groups()` returns its id columns.
- **Row closures.** A row closure receives `(Phibble\Row $row, Table $group)`.
  `$group` is the row's group, or the whole table when ungrouped.
- **Expressions.** Wherever a verb accepts a closure, it also accepts a
  `Phibble\Expr\Expr`, evaluated per group with the semantics in the
  [expression reference](expr.qmd).
- **Errors.** An unknown column name throws
  `Phibble\Exception\ColumnNotFound`.
- **Countable and iterable.** `count()` equals `nrow()`, and iterating yields
  one `Phibble\Row` per row.

## Methods

### Shape and data

| Method | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `columns()` | Column names in order. |
| `types()` | Column name to `Phibble\Type`. |
| `nrow()`, `ncol()` | Row and column counts. |
| `column($name)` | One column as a list. Factors return their labels. |
| `toRows()` | A list of associative arrays. |
| `toColumns()` | An array of lists by column name. |
| `collect()` | The rows as an in-memory `Frame`. A `Frame` returns itself. |

### Verbs

| Method | Semantics |
| --- | --- |
| `select($names)` | Keeps the named columns in the given order. Grouping columns are always kept. |
| `filter($predicate)` | Keeps rows where the closure or expression is true. NA counts as false. |
| `filterGroups($fn)` | Runs `$fn` once per group with the group's table. It returns one value per row, and truthy values keep the row. |
| `mutate($columns)` | Adds or replaces columns. A value is a row closure, an expression, a list with one value per row, or a scalar. Later entries see earlier ones. Replaced columns keep their position. |
| `mutateGroups($columns)` | Like `mutate()`, but a closure runs once per group and returns a list for the group's rows or a scalar. This is the primitive for window functions. |
| `rename($map)` | Renames columns, with `new => old` entries as in dplyr. |
| `arrange($keys)` | Sorts stably. Keys are names, <code>[name, &#39;asc&#39;&#124;&#39;desc&#39;]</code> pairs, or expressions, and NA sorts last in both directions. It ignores grouping. |
| `groupBy($names)`, `ungroup()`, `groups()` | Set, clear, or read the grouping columns. |
| `rowwise($idColumns)`, `isRowwise()` | Set or read rowwise mode. `groupBy()` and `ungroup()` clear it. |
| `eachGroup()` | Yields `['key' => [...], 'table' => Table]` for each group, with ungrouped tables. An ungrouped table yields one group with an empty key. |
| `summarise($aggregates)` | Returns one row per group: the keys, then one column per entry. Each entry is a closure given the group's table or an expression of size 1. The result drops the last grouping level, and a rowwise table keeps its id columns. The optional second argument is dplyr's `.groups`: `'drop_last'` (the default), `'drop'`, `'keep'`, or `'rowwise'`. |
| `distinct($names)` | Keeps the first row of each combination of the named columns (and the grouping columns), and only those columns. An empty list means all columns. |
| `take($indices)` | Rows by 0-based position, in the given order. A `null` index gives an all-NA row. Keeps types, factor levels, and grouping. |
| `slice($offset, $length)`, `head($n)` | Rows by position. These ignore grouping. |
| `join($other, $by, $type, ...)` | Joins with dplyr 1.1 semantics, described below. |

### Joins

`join()` takes the other table, a list of `[leftColumn, rightColumn]` key
pairs, and the join type: `inner`, `left`, `right`, `full`, `semi`, `anti`, or
`cross`. A bare column name means the same name on both sides, and a cross join
takes no keys.

- **Columns.** The result has x's columns, then y's columns other than its keys.
  Clashing names get the suffixes, `.x` and `.y` by default. With `keep: true`,
  y's keys are kept too.
- **Keys.** Without `keep`, the key columns come from x. For rows that only y
  has (right and full joins), they are filled from y's keys.
- **Rows.** Rows follow x's order, and each x row's matches follow y's order.
  Right and full joins then add y's unmatched rows in y's order. Semi and anti
  joins keep x's rows and columns and never duplicate rows.
- **Matching.** NA keys match each other unless `naMatches: false`. `1` matches
  `1.0`, and a factor matches text by its label.
- **Options.** `multiple` picks `all`, `any`, `first`, or `last` match per x
  row. `relationship` (`one-to-one`, `one-to-many`, `many-to-one`, or
  `many-to-many`) throws when the data violates it. Without it, an unexpected
  many-to-many join raises a warning, as dplyr does. `unmatched: 'error'`
  throws when the join would drop rows.
- **Grouping.** The result keeps x's grouping.

## Errors and allowed differences

`Frame` follows R, and other backends match it. The following rules apply
where R raises an error or where exact agreement is impractical.

- `quantile()` and `iqr()` over values that include NA, without
  `na_rm: true`, throw an error, as R does. A backend must not return NA.
- A summary entry that is not size 1 throws `LengthException`, and the message
  mentions `reframe()`.
- Aggregates over zero rows may return NA. `Frame` returns R's values (`NaN`
  for `mean()`, `Inf` and `-Inf` for `min()` and `max()`). This case only arises
  for an ungrouped table with no rows.
- `as_string()` on doubles with very large or very small magnitudes may
  differ from R's scientific notation. `Phibble\Column\Infer::formatFloat()`
  states R's rule: 15 significant digits, in fixed or scientific notation,
  whichever is shorter.

## Testing a backend

The simplest test of a backend is to run the same operations on the backend
and on `Frame` and compare the results. `tests/SqlTest.php` does this for
`SqlTable`. It loads the same data into a database, runs each operation both
ways, and compares the collected rows. It also runs every case in
`tests/fixtures/expr/expected.json`, the dplyr results that `tests/r/expr.R`
produces, so each backend is checked against R as well as against `Frame`.
